DataStax Builds Trust in Product Usage Data with Telmai
DataStax builds trust in product usage data with Telmai
Fully automated data observability empowers trust in product usage data across 36,000 clusters.
High quality data that feeds business KPIs on product usage metrics

With a growing number of customers and the strategic nature of their cloud offering, DataStax has an extremely high bar for data quality, and this includes the quality of product analytics data that is used for decision-making.

DataStax’s product usage analytics is collected from their database logs. DataStax’s data engineering team – led by Ankush Gautam – uses Python, DBT, and SQL to transform the data from log files into Google BigQuery tables. Tableau is then used for analytics and reporting.

Even with a strong data quality framework in place, SQL and Python data pipelines that read and transform log data into analytic-ready datasets were still prone to sporadic and unexpected issues. Any change in the upstream data transformation or the log data itself could create unexpected outliers in reporting and the metrics associated with it.

However, to track data quality at scale, DataStax needed a different approach and started to look for a solution that automates their process and is able to examine and investigate the actual data values and content.

at scale, the team decided to invest in the ML-based data observability solution of Telmai. With this automation, the high-caliber data engineering team could put their focus and resources on their core product advancement and leave the observability and monitoring to Telmai.
Today, Telmai monitors the actual data values, drifts, and anomalies in DataStax’s product usage. With Telmai, DataStax tracks
Observe drifts in volume/record count of clusters and investigate those records using a visual, no code data investigator product
Detect usage drifts on total read and total write compared to the predicted thresholds
ML anomaly detection and prediction of future quality issues

1) Patent and Intellectual Property Portfolio Analysis

TEL has a strong track record in areas such as "number of inventions created" and "patent application/grant rates." For example, in fiscal year 2024, it generated 1,331 inventions domestically and 296 overseas, maintaining a global patent application rate of approximately 75% for the last six consecutive years. (

This strength in intellectual property serves as a differentiator for TEL to build long-term relationships with customers even after equipment sales. In other words, it is easy for them to have an advantage in "solution provision" that includes not only the equipment itself but also peripheral technologies, process control, and software algorithms.

In other words, TEL's competitive positioning is characterized by "having strengths in a wide range of front-end equipment and peripheral process equipment, and securing a high market share in equipment other than lithography." (

include the fact that earnings are prone to fluctuation due to the volatility of the equipment sales cycle (capital investment cycle), and that market evaluation (stock price/valuation) is not settled as being undervalued or overvalued compared to competitors. (

Semiconductor processes are advancing in areas such as "miniaturization," "3D structuring," and "advanced packaging," and equipment manufacturers are required to evolve their equipment and process technologies in line with these trends.

In response to these trends, TEL is strengthening its front-end equipment such as coater/developers, cleaning, deposition, and etching, and is providing solutions for demands such as 3D stacked memory, chiplet structures, and HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) support.

In addition, since the integration of "equipment + software + data analysis/autonomous operation control" rather than process equipment alone will be an important technology strategy in the future, it will be interesting to see if TEL can shift its technology roadmap in this direction.

Semiconductor equipment has an extremely complex supply chain structure, involving numerous specialized companies in areas such as components, precision parts, optical systems, vacuum technology, control software, and maintenance services. Within this structure, TEL possesses a global network that includes both domestic Japanese and overseas bases. (

A key strength is its strong collaboration with domestic Japanese component and material companies, as well as its presence in a domestic ecosystem capable of supplying 'high-precision, high-reliability' equipment.

However, there are also challenges such as global geopolitical risks, uneven distribution of component supplies, and intensifying competition in price and delivery times. In particular, the regional bias in capital investment and dependence on specific component manufacturers can create vulnerabilities in the supply chain.
